extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of Stoicism; general readers wanting to apply Stoic philosophy in daily life
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for embodying Stoic theory in everyday life: social roles, emotional management (representation test), cosmopolitan attitudes, daily self-examination, and methods for internalizing Stoic maxims. Includes stepwise tests, habits, and reading/writing practices to form a personal handbook of Stoicism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions should not be anti-social and must contribute to the common good
rubrics_metrics.description: In simple terms, we will achieve this if our actions are not (1) anti-social and (2) contribute to the common good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-social actions include crimes and attitudes that harm the common good (from serious crimes to littering and rudeness). Actions that collaborate for the common good are those undertaken by those who perceive themselves as true members of a community (striving in profession, fulfilling family and social roles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fulfill assigned social, familial, and professional roles well
rubrics_metrics.description: We collaborate for the common good to the exact extent that we adequately fulfill the roles assigned to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a small-business owner benefits the community by managing the company well, creating jobs, and offering good services. Marcus Aurelius: 'what is not good for the beehive cannot be good for the bee.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice benevolence and charity
rubrics_metrics.description: We were created for mutual aid and union; we feel happy when benefiting someone, as we fulfill our own nature through such acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seneca: 'What virtue do we admire more than benevolence?' Cultivate benevolence as an expression of Stoic brotherhood of the human race.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cosmopolitanism: respect plurality while upholding justice and equity
rubrics_metrics.description: A Stoic’s benevolent and impartial view: acknowledge plurality of customs and religions but recognize justice and equity as common aspirations enabling peaceful interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoics lived in diverse societies and allowed ancestral customs to persist (Epictetus). The Stoic intervenes only when strictly necessary and per their social roles; they respect cultural diversity without descending into relativism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not coerce others into philosophy; moral development must be voluntary
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical exercise must be carried out uncoerced; the practitioner should do or refrain only when they know the reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoics propound teachings but explain them only to those who seek them freely; training that ignores enlightenment is not proper action of a free human being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead by example; do not flaunt philosophical principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Never declare yourself a philosopher nor speak frequently with those ignorant of philosophy about principles—do the things that follow from these principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At a banquet, do not say how one should eat, but eat as one should. Socrates tolerated being disregarded so that those genuinely interested would come—and he would lead by action rather than speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid moral judgment without understanding another's premises
rubrics_metrics.description: We can only judge someone morally if we know the premises that lead them to act or think in one way or another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek to know their beliefs, upbringing, cultural context and era. Instead of recrimination, pursue benevolent understanding (Epictetus: someone bathes hastily—say 'hastily', not 'badly').

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation test — Stage 1: give yourself time (delay assent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first stage: giving oneself time—waiting for the intensity of the representation to decrease so that reason can confront it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count to three; initial passionate impulses subside after time. If acted on hastily, a passionate movement becomes a passion and reason is overwhelmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation test — Stage 2: separate sensory data from judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The second stage: separate sensory data from the judgment made about it and suspend value judgments based on intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize whether the perception concerns something under your control; if not, treat it as 'nothing to me' and refrain from assigning intrinsic value—this prepares for the next stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation test — Stage 3: select an appropriate virtue to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: The third stage: select a virtue (excellence/arete) to deal with the object of intense representation (e.g., self-control for sexual attraction, perseverance for exhaustive tasks, patience for insult).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Habituate these modes so representations do not drag you down. Epictetus: 'Regarding everything that happens to you, remember, turning to yourself, to seek some excellence that serves for each of them.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a habit (hexis/ethos) of examining representations and choosing virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a stable disposition to examine representations and select the appropriate virtue for recurring situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because passionate movements continually reach the soul, repeated practice and habit make it easier to face difficult situations properly when they arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain equanimity when consoling others—help without being carried away
rubrics_metrics.description: When witnessing others' distress, do not be carried away into the same suffering; instead, have solidarity in words and, if necessary, mourn with them but avoid inward lamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a doctor should not despair with a grieving mother; the doctor must remain inwardly steady to use knowledge and save the patient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despise things not under your control to avoid envy and preserve freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be carried away by the belief that honors, power, or reputation equal happiness; if the good lies in things under our control, there is no room for envy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to be a free person, not a general or consul; true happiness is acting virtuously and independence from externals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accustom yourself to the transient nature of people and possessions
rubrics_metrics.description: To deal virtuously with things and loved ones, accustom yourself to accepting their transience—e.g., rehearse that possessions and loved ones may be returned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you kiss your child or wife, tell yourself they are human; when they die you will not be disturbed. This premeditation reduces emotional disturbance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the nature and purpose of actions; keep intention aligned with nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Before undertaking a task, inquire about its nature and fix your will accordingly; do not let incidental obstacles divert your intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: going to public baths—expect bumping, insults, theft; determine 'I want to bathe and maintain my will according with nature' so obstacles won't cause annoyance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat death as not inherently evil; distress arises from opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Death itself is not an evil; it is the opinion that makes it terrible—disturbance is due to our own beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When hindered or distressed, attribute it to your opinions rather than external events; regulate judgments to avoid needless suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not boast about externals; value is in the use of representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not exalt yourself for possessions (e.g., a beautiful horse); exalt yourself for the use of representations—how you act in accordance with nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your worth stems from virtuous use of representations; when using them according to nature, you can justifiably praise yourself for your own good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ready to abandon non-essential things when duty calls
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep attention on the primary object (the ship) and be prepared to abandon shells and fish (accessories) when the captain calls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: on a voyage, be continuously oriented to the ship so you can respond immediately; likewise in life be ready to leave non-essentials for duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illness and bodily hindrances do not remove the will’s capacity—invoke relevant virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Disease is an obstacle for the body, but not for the will if it chooses not to be hindered; treat physical obstacles as separate from the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke virtues such as perseverance, patience, and courage to confront illness and bodily limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider possessions and relationships as lent rather than lost
rubrics_metrics.description: Never say you 'lost' something; say it was 'returned'—this reframes attachment and reduces distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a son or wife dies or property is taken, consider it returned to its source; the question of who took it is irrelevant to your proper attitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against seductive pleasures—delay and compare future regret
rubrics_metrics.description: When tempted by pleasure, grant yourself time and imagine two moments: enjoyment and subsequent regret; compare and choose abstention if it yields greater self-praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the representation wait, anticipate future criticism, and weigh long-term victory over immediate sweetness. But if the opportune moment truly arises, beware letting seduction overcome you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unmask false appearances; know the real nature of things and act virtuously
rubrics_metrics.description: Go beyond mere appearance to understand the real nature of each thing; the sage knows reality and thus can act appropriately and virtuously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify things that seem good but are not, and those that seem evil but are not; this knowledge links to virtue and leads to a happy life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily examination of conscience (nightly review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review each day's actions before sleep: what was done wrong, what accomplished, what remains to do; take responsibility for errors and rejoice for right actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice introspective investigation (Pythagorean/Platonic tradition). Seneca and Epictetus recommend nightly meditation to assess against the standard of virtue and plan improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep Stoic maxims at hand: read, underline, paraphrase, and synthesize
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the main maxims of Stoicism 'at the tip of the tongue' by reading ancient texts, underlining important parts, jotting them down, and paraphrasing into your own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After reading, transcribe underlined parts into a notebook, add personal observations, revisit and paraphrase repeatedly to internalize an inner discourse in harmony with reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to embody theoremata (Stoic principles) rather than seek erudition
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective of reading and note-taking is to embody philosophical principles and progress to virtuous action—not to become merely erudite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Socrates’ example of questioning oneself and exercising critical thought in solitude; internalization leads to action rather than rhetorical composition.
